1	---
2	name: spec-author
3	description: Use to start a new product spec, add a feature to an existing spec, or keep a spec in sync with behavior changes. Setting a project up on live-spec comes earlier, at build-pipeline's setup entry. Documenting already-built code after the fact and a prototype sketch that carries no spec stay outside it.
4	metadata:
5	  version: 5.0.0
6	---
7	
8	# Spec Author
9	
10	> Part of the **live-spec pack** — the shared working rules (ask-never-guess · plain words, anchors trail ·
11	> one surface = one name · one home per fact · junior/senior split · checkpoints · the concurrent-edit
12	> fence · freshness · journal discipline · attic-never-delete · verify by deed · the human's gates · claims
13	> need primary sources · fix the class, sweep look-alikes · the door before code · prototype ≠ product) live once in the pack's base skill, `live-spec-base` (v5.0.0), together with the
14	> settings ladder — this skill references them and elaborates only its own domain. That base skill's
15	> file is `skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md`, and it states each of those rules in full. Loaded without
16	> it, this page still runs every section below. What it loses is those shared rules and the settings
17	> ladder, which live in that base skill alone.
18	
19	spec-author authors and grows a **living spec** — a requirements-genre `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` that says what the product is, what every
20	part is allowed to claim, and how the parts compose — *incrementally, as the project develops*. spec-author is the
21	front half of a pair: **spec-author writes the spec; [`product-prover`](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec/tree/main/skills/product-prover)
22	reviews it.** A spec written this way should be one the prover can check: same primitives, surfaces named once,
23	cross-links explicit.
24	
25	spec-author's job is to keep a spec that is **complete for what exists, honest about what's undecided, and
26	structured so the prover can find the holes the author can't** — grown as the work grows, never front-loaded
27	as a giant document.
28	
29	## Words this skill uses
30	
31	**Where the paths in this file point.** Two trees are in play. The named files under `scripts/`,
32	`guardrails/`, `templates/`, `tests/`, and `skills/` are the live-spec pack's own, at
33	`github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. So are the design notes this page names by filename under
34	`docs/`. An install copies each skill folder into one place, so a path naming another skill points to
35	that skill's folder, beside this skill's folder. Every other path belongs to the project the pack is
36	attached to, including `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `JOURNAL.md`, and
37	`.live-spec/`.
38	
39	Run every script named below from the live-spec repository root, as `python3 <path> <arguments>`. Each
40	one prints its own usage line when it is run with no arguments, so the arguments never have to be
41	guessed.
42	
43	- **Wish** — one request a person voices in plain words, captured as a queue row.
44	- **Door** — the intake classification that sends a queued wish to one entry point of the pipeline. Its
45	  values are feature, bug, refactor, docs-only, and skip. It is decided before any code is written.
46	- **Queue row** — one row of the project's queue, `ROADMAP.md` in this pack. A closed row moves to
47	  `docs/queue-archive/`, so a row number cited below may sit there rather than in the live queue.
48	- **Lane** — one build train a session rolls through the pipeline.
49	- **Landing** — one piece of work reaching the repository's shared truth as one commit.
50	- **Host** — one project the pack attaches to. Each host keeps its own spec, queue, journal, and
51	  `.live-spec/` folder.
52	- **Host profile** — the host's own settings file, `.live-spec/profile.md`. This page reads its
53	  `project.kind`, `project.layers`, `project.design-principles`, and `project.axes` lines.
54	- **Kind** — what a host's product is, named from a fixed vocabulary: book, backend service, static
55	  site, fullstack app, CLI, or skill pack. The host profile records it.
56	- **Surface** — any part of the shipped product a user meets. A **stateful surface** holds state a
57	  user can change and find again later.
58	- **Spec-delta** — the set of spec sentences one wish or feature adds or changes.
59	- **Facet** — one aspect of a feature's design, ending as a written spec sentence.
60	- **Regression fence** — one sentence in a spec-delta naming a neighbouring promise that must stay
61	  true through the change, citing the clause it guards.
62	- **Composition axis** — one angle a stateful surface's behaviour can vary along.
63	- **Lens** — one named check the prover or the design review walks a document with.
64	- **Seat** — the session that orchestrates the work and reports to the person.
65	- **Red**, used as a verb — a check fails and stops the work at that point.
66	
67	**The markers this page writes.** `[feature: F-x]` on a requirement heading marks a person-facing
68	scenario. `[target]` marks a surface or phase the spec names and does not yet specify for build.
69	`[default]` names a value the agent chose that the person may retune. `[GAP: ...]` under a criterion
70	records what the source left open. `⟨DECIDE⟩` marks a call only the person can make, and it carries a
71	one-line question.
72	
73	**The bracket codes.** `INV-`, `E-`, `T-`, `S-`, `C-`, `M-`, `D-`, `A-`, `B-`, and `ACT-` codes index
74	requirements in this pack's own `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`. Its preamble names each letter's kind: `E-` an
75	entity, `INV-` an invariant, `T-` a transition, `M-` a rhythm rule, `A-` an adoption step, `B-` a
76	bootstrap step, `ACT-` an actor, `C-` a composition-axis rule, `D-` a recorded decision, and `S-` a
77	header rule. `PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md` maps each code to the criteria carrying it, written as `R12.4` —
78	requirement 12, criterion 4. Each sentence beside a code states its own rule in full, so a reader
79	holding this page alone can pass the codes over.
80	
81	## Work that belongs elsewhere
82	
83	Reserve it for a spec the code will chase. Skip it for retro-documenting already-built code so it looks
84	specced (the spec leads, code chases), for a prototype (a sketch gets a label and a fence, never a spec),
85	for pure research notes, and for the skip-boundary edit (single file, no new behaviour — it goes straight
86	to code + its test); and reach for product-prover instead when what's wanted is a review — its half of the pair.
87	
88	## The one rule
89	
90	> A spec exists so the next reader — the prover, a teammate, or the author months later — can reason about
91	> every reachable situation. If a situation the system can reach isn't in the spec, the spec is incomplete,
92	> even if the code "works."
93	
94	## How it reads — human-first, in plain product language
95	
96	A spec is read by a **human first** (a teammate, the author months later) and a prover second — and both from
97	**one** document. Write it in the **language of the product**: plain words a product person speaks — what the
98	thing is and does, in whole sentences. Machine fragments with markup have no place in it. It doesn't have to read like a textbook/lesson either;
99	**product language is the register**, whatever fits the project. Don't fork a "readable" copy and a
100	"checkable" copy; they drift apart and one goes stale. The format below serves both at once. It was tested on a real
101	project: a prover-facing spec that read like "machine fragments with markup" was rejected by its author and
102	stopped being read, and a spec no one reads stops doing its job.
103	
104	- **The body is a list of requirements; each opens with its situation.** After the preamble and the
105	  glossary, the body is a list of requirements. A requirement is named by the situation it governs
106	  ("The spec keeps what is built apart from what is planned", "A wish is captured as a queue row that is
107	  never lost") and carries three parts in order: a **Context** block of two to four short sentences —
108	  when the situation arises, who is involved, what the reader sees; a one-sentence **User Story** — as a
109	  person in a named position, I want one thing, so that one benefit follows; and the **acceptance
110	  criteria**, the behaviour grouped into named cases. The reader meets the situation and the people in it
111	  before the first rule, and a term is introduced before a rule uses it. A person-facing requirement is
112	  also called a **scenario** — its heading carries a `[feature: F-x]` tag; a machinery or reference
113	  requirement is not a scenario.
114	- **Acceptance criteria group into named cases, one criterion carrying one trigger and one response.** A
115	  **case** is one bold line naming a situation ("**Case: a wish becomes a row at once**"), followed by two
116	  to six numbered criteria. Every criterion sits in exactly one case, and the numbering runs continuously
117	  through the requirement. The keywords *when*, *while*, *if*, *then*, and *shall* are set in lowercase
118	  italics: *shall* states a duty, *when* and *while* open a situation, *if* opens a condition and *then*
119	  its result. No word in the document is written in all capitals outside a code anchor or a filename. A
120	  guardrail holds this shape — `guardrails/check-requirement-shape.py` reds a requirement missing its
121	  Context, its User Story, or its `### Acceptance Criteria`, and a criterion whose case or anchor is wrong.
122	  The parser behind that guardrail reads fixed line forms, held in `guardrails/specformat.py`:
123	    - a requirement heading opens `## Requirement N: `;
124	    - the Context line opens `**Context:**`, and the story line opens `**User Story:**`;
125	    - the criteria sit under a `### Acceptance Criteria` heading, each one written `N. text`;
126	    - a case line reads `**Case: the situation**`, bold and alone on its line;
127	    - a glossary entry reads `- **term** — definition`.
128	- **Each scenario states how it is entered and how it exits (SPEC INV-127).** A scenario is a flow with
129	  edges, and its Context block carries them: it states how the situation arises — from which prior state,
130	  with what already true (the preconditions) — and what the situation leaves true when it resolves (the
131	  postcondition). An entry or exit that is trivially none — a top-level scenario entered from nowhere, a
132	  terminal one exiting to nowhere — is stated in one short clause, so a reader tells a decided edge from
133	  an overlooked one. The duty binds forward: a new scenario carries its edges from the first draft, and
134	  product-prover flags an existing scenario's unstated edge as a finding (its scenario-level
135	  precondition/postcondition lens, kin of the entry-symmetry lens INV-50).
136	- **The criteria carry the meaning; the machine handles stay quiet.** Every criterion is a plain sentence a
137	  person reads straight through. The short codes — `[INV-18]`, `[T-1]`, `[E-3]` — trail at the **end** of the
138	  line as quiet handles for the prover and the test matrix. A reader skims past them; the maintainer follows
139	  them. **Never open a criterion with its code.** A range such as `[T-1..T-7]` cites its whole run of codes
140	  in one anchor.
141	- **A generated code-to-location table closes the doc.** The spec closes with a `## Reference` section
142	  holding one table that maps every code its criteria carry → the requirement-and-criterion locations that
143	  carry it (for example `INV-1` → `R4.3, R4.4, R5.1`). The table is **generated output**, built from the
144	  body criteria by `scripts/build-index.py`; no one edits it by hand, and feature codes (`F-...`) live on
145	  their scenario headings and take no table row. The authored home of each code's plain statement is its
146	  criterion in the body and its noun in the glossary; the table carries locations only. The gate
147	  `guardrails/check-index-generated.py` reds a committed table that differs from a fresh build, a body code
148	  the table misses, or a table code no criterion carries — so the table can never drift into a second truth.
149	  Two commands work it. `python3 scripts/build-index.py PRODUCT_SPEC.md -o PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md` builds
150	  the table, and that output is spliced under `## Reference`. `python3
151	  guardrails/check-index-generated.py PRODUCT_SPEC.md PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md` then reads the document
152	  beside its committed copy.
153	- **Name the situation in the case; put the exact threshold in the criterion.** The bold **case** line
154	  names the situation in plain words; the numbered criteria under it carry the exact number or condition.
155	  The reader gets the shape from the case; the builder drops into the criterion for the precise value.
156	- **Use lists inside a Context block or a criterion to break up a wall of prose.** The acceptance criteria
157	  are already a numbered list by construction; this rule governs the prose around them. When a Context block
158	  or a criterion spells out several forms, legs, or arms — a label's forms, a check's three legs, a law's
159	  four arms — lay them out as bullet or numbered items so the eye scans them, and keep prose for the
160	  reasoning that connects them.
161	- **The enumeration threshold makes that checkable (SPEC INV-215).** A prose paragraph carrying an
162	  enumeration of three or more distinct, parallel facts earns bullet or numbered structure — a filename
163	  rule with its collision law and its header fields and its body parts, run together in one paragraph, is
164	  a list the reader should scan, so lay the members out as items. Prose stays for the laws, their reasoning,
165	  and their boundaries; the enumeration of parallel members becomes the list. This stays a stated writing
166	  rule, read by eye and by the prover's cognitive-load lens, and it earns no mechanical lint. A regex
167	  flagging every three-comma sentence would trip on ordinary rhetorical triads — a neutral, precise, plain
168	  register, or a rule with its actor and its reason. Telling a genuine list-owed enumeration from a
169	  rhetorical triad is a meaning call the register judge and the prover make, past a regex's reach. The rule
170	  came from the owner, 2026-07-17, reading the promoter's inter-agent design doc: a paragraph packing a
171	  filename rule, a collision law, three header fields, and four body parts belongs in a bulleted list —
172	  the human language was already right, and the one remaining fix was reading efficiency.
173	- **A preamble and a glossary open the doc.** Open the spec with a short preamble: what the document covers
174	  in two or three sentences, what the bracket codes are (each letter's kind, taken from the list under
175	  "The bracket codes" above — and that a reader can ignore them while a maintainer follows
176	  them), how the keywords *shall*, *when*, *while*, *if*, and *then* read, and that **edit history lives in
177	  the JOURNAL, apart from the spec itself.** A **glossary** follows, before the first requirement: every
178	  domain noun the body uses carries a one-sentence entry there, defined once under one name (closed
179	  vocabulary — a coined word is translated to a defined standard term before it enters the document). The
180	  gate `guardrails/check-vocabulary.py` reds a term defined twice, a glossary entry no body line uses,
181	  and a coinage listed in `guardrails/spec-coinages.json`. Its own header states what it leaves out.
182	  No script can tell a domain noun from ordinary English, so a used-but-undefined noun is caught by
183	  the cold reader instead.
184	- **The spec states the current truth — a changelog lives elsewhere.** No "changed in v0.8.3 from…" edit-history notes in the prose;
185	  the *why-we-changed-it* belongs in `JOURNAL.md` (dated, with the reason). A superseded rule may stay with a
186	  one-line "superseded by §X" pointer when the old shape still needs explaining — but the prose reads as
187	  today's truth.
188	- **Layer overview up front.** If the spec stacks layers (a credibility floor, then features on top), open
189	  with a 3–5 line "how the layers stack" map so a reader always knows where they are.
190	- **Readable-first beats terse.** Clipped machine-fragment prose gets rejected by humans as hard as a wall of
191	  fluff does. Err toward a sentence that *reads well*; keep the structure, lose the jargon. Terseness is not
192	  the goal. The goal is a headline the eye lands on, then detail it can drill into.
193	- **Write in the pack's technical-writer register.** Spec prose reads like a native-English open-source
194	  technical writer: neutral, precise, easy to follow. The full register (define abstract terms in plain
195	  words at first use, one term per concept, concrete nouns, active voice, cut nominalizations and filler,
196	  metaphors only as one-off color) and the per-section verification checklist live once in the
197	  `communicator` skill's writing register — `skills/communicator/references/writing-register.md` (its home
198	  since row 266) — spec prose follows it like every other human-facing text.
199	- **A machine gate holds the register — attention alone drifts — and the prose is written by a clean agent.**
200	  Re-styling a spec by hand drifts (a voice reads fine on a sample, then the same tells return round after
201	  round). A **tell** here is a writing habit a reader recognizes as machine-written. The durable fix has
202	  five parts, and parts 2 to 5 are proven and sealed in `docs/prose-quality-gate-design.md`:
203	    1. A fresh agent with the pack not loaded writes the prose from bare facts. A context that has
204	       loaded the pack writes ornate prose, so it only does the mechanical half. This leg is spec law
205	       (SPEC INV-84), restated in `skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md`.
206	    2. `scripts/spec-style-lint.py --gate` blocks the tells a regex can see: contrast-by-denial frames,
207	       define-by-exclusion openers, jargon, shouted capitals, second person, reassurance, and future
208	       narration. Defined terms are allowlisted and marked informative regions are exempt.
209	    3. `scripts/spec-redundancy-precheck.py` catches lexical near-duplication. `scripts/spec-judge.py`
210	       then runs a fresh language-model judge against the hash-pinned rubric `scripts/judge-rubric.md`,
211	       for the redundancy and register a regex cannot see.
212	    4. An unfixed tell is recorded in `scripts/spec-waivers.json` as a dated waiver, and the running
213	       total is capped by `scripts/spec-debt-cap.json`.
214	    5. `scripts/spec-done-gate.py` is the one definition of done.
215	
216	  Restyle each section through this loop: fresh writer → gate to 0 errors → anchor multiset
217	  unchanged → suite green → re-point any broken traceability check-phrase by narrowing to a register-clean phrase
218	  (log it) → commit. The floor is the machine; the ceiling stays the exemplars + a human's read.
219	
220	This is the shape `product-prover` is tuned to read, and the one a human will actually keep open.
221	
222	## Shipped docs state each requirement impersonally
223	
224	A shipped product doc — the spec, the test matrix, the README, a skill card — is read by everyone the project reaches: a contributor, an auditor, a future user, a reader months later. Write each requirement as three plain parts: the rule, the actor as a role (the user, the producer, the target user), and the reason it holds. The reason is load-bearing and stays; the personal attribution drops, and a dated decision keeps the date as a plain anchor and drops the name — "chosen 2026-07-06 for a cold-start reader" carries what the next reader can act on, and a person's name gives them nothing to act on.
225	
226	For that reason, personal attribution and candid process voice have one home: the local-only diaries, the JOURNAL and NEXT_STEPS, which no publish ships. Who decided a thing, and a session's own frank notes about how it went, belong there — the shipped clause carries the rule and its reason, the diary carries the story. Write the shipped clause impersonally from the first draft; do not scrub names at publish time, and let the publish floor stand only as the backstop. (SPEC INV-118.)
227	
228	## The spine — what every spec must contain (not its section order)
229	
230	The spine is a completeness checklist: it constrains what the document contains, and the section order
231	stays free. The document is organized as a glossary
232	followed by a list of requirements (per "How it reads" and `templates/PRODUCT_SPEC.template.md`); each spine
233	item lives inside a requirement's criteria, or — for a domain noun — in the glossary, and every code is
234	findable through the generated code-to-location table. Never let a new feature land without its entry.
235	
236	1. **Purpose** — why the product exists, in plain words: the opening preamble.
237	2. **Entities** — the nouns. Each defined in the **glossary**, with its attributes, its unit/valid range if
238	   it's a measure, and its **states** if it has a lifecycle. *One concept, one name* (see below).
239	3. **States & transitions** — every move an entity can make, told as criteria (which action, which actor,
240	   what triggers it). A state with no way out is a bug; say what exits it.
241	4. **Actors** — who initiates each significant action (user, role, automated service, external system).
242	   "Who does this?" must have an answer for every transition.
243	5. **Invariants** — the properties that must hold across *every* reachable state, stated as criteria that
244	   hold while the situation runs. Cover both sides:
245	   - **Safety** — what must never happen (mutually-exclusive modes, no over-claiming, no partial writes).
246	   - **Liveness** — what must eventually happen (every async path completes / times out / rolls back).
247	6. **Cross-section composition** — the part most specs miss. See the dedicated step below.
248	7. **Terms** — every domain term is defined in the glossary, once, under one name. A word of ordinary
249	   English needs no entry.
250	
251	Mark anything that needs a human's domain call with **⟨DECIDE⟩** and a one-line question. Never invent
252	intent to fill a gap — flag it.
253	
254	**Name the future with the [target] tag — it is a tripwire that drives the pipeline.** A surface or phase the
255	spec names but does not yet specify for build carries the literal tag `[target]` (the header's
256	current-vs-target paragraph lists them). That tag is the canonical, machine-checkable form of "not yet
257	specified / later surface": the pipeline's feature tripwires key off it — touching a [target] surface
258	starts at the spec step, full stop (SPEC S-0, INV-16). Plain-prose phrasings (`TBD`, "future work",
259	"planned") bind too, but always write the tag: a future the machine can't see is a future a session can
260	hand-build past the method.
261	
262	**A clause born of an approved look points at its norm (SPEC INV-43).** When the human approves a
263	visual prototype as the look ("this is the door"), the clause that encodes it carries a `norm: <path>`
264	pointer at its line end, beside its anchors — the prose carries the laws, the artifact keeps the look;
265	a build from text alone ships a cheap look-alike with a green suite (tlvphotos, 2026-07-05). Approval
266	freezes the artifact into the project's records: copy it to `docs/norms/` with a dated provenance line
267	(what, approved when, from which sketch) and point at the frozen copy, keeping the one-way fence absolute
268	— the prototype's code sits in its own named home, and nothing in the shipped product reaches into it
269	(E-17); a pointer into a live prototype home would break it. A text-born clause carries no pointer, and the law
270	binds forward — a clause owes its pointer at the first landing that touches it.

272	**Reshaping an existing spec? Hold the anchor-set guard.** A restructure (a genre migration, a resection)
273	must carry exactly the prior anchor set: diff the sorted anchor list before and after — identical sets prove
274	the shape changed and no rule was lost; any delta must be a deliberate, named change. Do not renumber or
275	retire a code as a side effect of a restructure; where a rule genuinely changes home, keep its anchor and
276	state today's home.

278	## The move most specs miss: compose every stateful surface across every axis
279	
280	This move catches the bugs that pass every unit test, and a feature-focused author skips it.
281	
282	When a surface (a player, a form, an editor, a panel) carries **state**, the system almost always also has
283	**global axes** it renders under. This is the **canonical axis list — its home is here; other docs point at it:**
284	
285	- **view** (compact / detailed) · **mode** (quick / full, read / edit) · **tier** · **viewport size** ·
286	  **persistence / reopen** (any state that survives a reload — localStorage, a saved file) ·
287	  **concurrency** where it applies ·
288	  **every other live surface** — every other surface that can be present at the same time, whether or not
289	  that other surface holds state: a sibling sharing the screen, or a surface the flow reaches just before
290	  or after this one (a static end screen counts). For each, state what this surface does while that one is
291	  present: hold, clear, or hand off.
292	
293	The bugs that pass every unit test live in the **product** of surface-state × axis, because each was
294	specified alone. The three authors forget most: viewport size (a grid that reflows below some width),
295	persistence/reopen (state written last session auto-restoring into a changed UI), and every other live
296	surface (a caption still naming the previous photo once the closing screen arrives, because "what the
297	caption shows when the finale is in view" was never written).
298	
299	So, for every stateful surface, before its section is called done:
300	
301	- **Enumerate it against each global axis.** For each axis value (each view/mode/tier), state what happens
302	  to the surface's state and controls. Is the state still *visible*? Still *reversible*? Does the axis
303	  transition *preserve, reset, or block* the state?
304	- **Name the composition invariant.** e.g. *"a per-stem mute/solo is reachable only while its control
305	  surface is visible; entering the compact view resets to the full mix."* Without it, the
306	  stranding bug follows: a state set in one view, hidden by another, with no way to see or undo it.
307	- **One surface, one name.** If the player's lanes and the `#stemlanes` canvas are the same thing, call
308	  them the same thing everywhere. A reviewer (human or prover) can only connect a cross-section hole when
309	  both sides are named identically and present in the same document — two names for one surface hides the
310	  seam.
311	- **If the surface persists state, compose the versions too.** When it writes localStorage/disk, enumerate
312	  version-N-1 state × version-N code explicitly: what does the current UI do when it reads a stored value
313	  that's older, partial, or belongs to a since-removed feature? State a migrate / ignore / clear rule — this
314	  is the seam behind "reopened it and it looked broken".

329	Author in this order; every part below is mandatory for a feature and no scope cut may trim it
330	(scope dials richness; it never trims the safety net — SPEC T-15):
331	
332	1. **Regression fences** — when the wish touches a live surface (next section; SPEC T-14, INV-19);
333	2. **The new behaviour itself** — entities, states, transitions, composed across the canonical axes;
334	3. **The standard-facet sweep** — every facet a spec sentence, decided or `[default]`-tagged (SPEC T-13, INV-18);
335	4. **The fit walk** — how the feature sits in the person's path, kind-scaled (SPEC INV-29);

340	## The regression fences — run first when the wish touches a surface that already lives (SPEC T-14, INV-19)
341	
342	Before authoring anything new, preserve the neighbours. The spec-delta opens with one sentence per
343	existing promise that must stay true through the change ("the catalog still opens on click"), each
344	citing the spec clause it guards. A fence is not new law and earns no new matrix row — the cited
345	clause's row already carries its never-side, and the landing's full-suite run is what proves the fence
346	held. Split what the delta touches: promises that stay are fenced; behaviour being changed is
347	re-authored as new law — a fact is fenced or re-authored, never both. A fence that finds no clause
348	behind it has discovered an unwritten promise: reconcile it from the shipped truth (like an adopted
349	claim), write it as its own spec fact with its own row, and state it explicitly. If
350	the cited neighbour claim is adoption-born and still unverified, its reconciliation runs before it can
351	be fenced — a hope cannot be fenced. Name the fences by cited anchor in the wish's queue row, which is
352	a row of `ROADMAP.md` in this pack ("fences: …"), so "untouched and still true" stays searchable. A
353	prototype fences nothing — it promises

502	## The delta's two closing sentences — non-goals and the success measure (SPEC INV-20, INV-21)
503	
504	Every feature's spec-delta closes with two short sentences, always written; neither may be
505	left out. **Non-goals**: what is deliberately left out ("version comparison waits for a later pass");
506	"nothing deliberately left out this time" is itself valid — only a missing sentence is a hole, and a
507	non-goal that narrows what the wish asked for rides the batched report, never a silent narrowing.
508	**A success measure**: how we'd notice the feature worked for its person, a number where one exists;
509	decided or `[default]`-tagged — the tag marks provenance only, no test row derives from it until the
510	reading machinery lands. The quantification questions (analytics tag? how measured? A/B worth it?) ride
511	the facet sweep's batched report. Both bind forward; an adopted feature owes its pair at the first
512	landing that touches it. A prototype writes neither — it promises nothing.

514	## The primary unit — one per project type, traced end to end (SPEC E-29, INV-73)
515	
516	A spec has a primary unit: the thing the reader counts, the product's spine repeated. The unit is a
517	parameter of the project's type — the way a domain swaps a template — declared once, then it sets the
518	heading style, the acceptance-criterion shape, and what the coverage check means.
519	
520	| project type | primary unit | the coverage check validates |
521	|---|---|---|
522	| web / app | a user-facing **feature** (a visible flow) | every feature → architecture node(s) + a test |
523	| CLI / library / API | a **command** / function / endpoint | every surface → its contract, an owning module + a test |
524	| methodology package | a rule or **guarantee** the pack promises | every guarantee → an enforcing mechanism (a script, a gate, a template) |
525	| content / book / article | an **argument** / chapter / section | every promised argument → a home in the outline (a structure check; no technical architecture) |
526	
527	**The mechanic is one, for every type.** Each unit carries a stable inline tag on its heading — the same
528	family as the anchors, e.g. `[feature: F-wish]` — and the downstream artifacts back-reference it: one
529	coverage table in ARCHITECTURE.md names the implementer node(s) and a test per unit. The two-way check reads
530	both directions — every unit has an implementer and a test, and every promised unit carries its tag. In this
531	pack that check is the feature-coverage trace in `tests/test_traceability.py`, reading ARCHITECTURE.md's
532	`## Feature coverage` table. This
533	is the anchor-ownership machinery extended a level up, never a second machine to keep in sync.
534	
535	**No file explosion.** One PRODUCT_SPEC.md, one ARCHITECTURE.md, one TEST_MATRIX.md; the unit tags live
536	inline in the prose and the one coverage table binds them. Shard into per-feature files only for a
537	genuinely huge project, and only by explicit call.
538	
539	**The source is plain Markdown; the render resolves the links.** The source stays plain Markdown — a
540	tag plus one table. When a doc is rendered, a relative `.md` cross-link opens its rendered `.html`
541	neighbour and its `#anchor` lands on the target heading (ROADMAP row 195, shipped 2026-07-10). Linking
542	a trailing bracket code to its row in the code-to-location table stays an optional later leg; until that lands, a reader
543	follows a bare tag by searching the source.
544	
545	**On live-spec itself.** live-spec is a package, but its scenarios are the product's features, so it
546	dogfoods the web/app row: each person-facing scenario heading tags `[feature: F-x]` and the Feature
547	coverage table maps it to its skills and its test. The machines that work behind the scenes (guardrails,
548	host contract) implement guarantees; they are not user-facing features, and they stay outside the feature layer
549	by the type's own definition of its unit. The decided design note is `docs/spec-format-by-project-type.md`.
550	
551	**The heading convention makes the reverse direction mechanical (SPEC INV-132).** For the two-way check to
552	catch a scenario whose tag was forgotten, an untagged heading has to be unambiguous — and it is not on its
553	own, since the checker cannot tell a new scenario missing its tag from a machinery or reference section
554	that never had one. So every requirement heading — `## Requirement N: …`, the level every person-facing
555	scenario uses — carries either its `[feature: F-x]` tag (a person-facing scenario) or the explicit
556	`[not a scenario]` marker (a machinery, rules, or reference section, legitimately untagged), and an
557	untagged, unmarked requirement heading is unambiguously red. The parts under it — the `### Acceptance
558	Criteria` sub-heading and the bold case lines — nest inside a requirement already tagged or marked, so they
559	owe nothing. When a section that is not a person-facing scenario is added, state its `[not a scenario]`
560	marker in the same edit — a new machinery heading that passes silently is the gap this closes.

562	## The content contract — when a generic engine is extracted from an instance (SPEC INV-79)
563	
564	A generic engine carved out of a working project inherits the donor's assumptions silently: an id
565	format, a hardcoded wordmark, a path, a language default. At extraction the spec opens a **content
566	contract** section: every donor-specific constant the extraction finds becomes a named entry — what
567	the engine requires from any instance's content, in the engine's own vocabulary — and each entry
568	owes a test that the engine works without the donor's value (test-author's half of the same law).
569	An assumption with no entry is a leak the next instance discovers in production.

571	## Crossing the instance→engine boundary — provenance and naming (SPEC INV-119)
572	
573	A feature usually proves itself first on a live instance and then generalizes into the engine. When that history goes into the engine's spec, write it as the engine's own record: the reader is anyone who runs the engine, so every provenance handle points at something that reader can reach, and the spec reads as generic from the first line.
574	
575	Four conventions carry the boundary:
576	
577	- **The history reads as a reconciliation.** Head the history section "Reconciliation log — how each behaviour landed in code", and let each entry trace a behaviour to where it landed in the engine's own code. This is a spec-versus-code reconciliation the engine's reader can follow. It is not a fork's delta against an instance's reference implementation.
578	- **Provenance cites the engine's own public commit.** Each entry names where the behaviour landed in the engine — "landed in engine commit `<hash>`" — a commit any reader can check out in the engine's own history. A private instance's commit is invisible to that reader, so an instance hash stays out of the engine's provenance.
579	- **One intro sentence states the normal intake path, once.** Open the log with a single sentence naming the usual route — "Most rows record a feature proven first on a live instance and then generalized into the engine" — so no per-entry line re-explains where features come from.
580	- **A mechanism carries a neutral internal name; a visible instance label is marked as instance copy.** Name a mechanism by what it does in the engine's own vocabulary — "the unfold step", "the show-more control". Where a running instance shows locale-specific words for it, the spec notes that string as instance-supplied copy the instance plugs in [INV-79], and the neutral term stays the mechanism's one name [E-4].
581	
582	## Standard vocabulary — what our house terms map to
583	
584	The pack's method is its own, but its concepts are the field's, and naming the lineage lets a reader who
585	knows requirements engineering recognize what a live-spec document is doing. The crosswalk to the field's
586	vocabulary (`ISO`/arc42/C4) lives in `docs/spec-format-by-project-type.md`.
587	
588	Two boundaries the crosswalk does not erase: our spec stays a single requirements-genre document — a
589	glossary and a body of requirements — and a term joins our vocabulary only when it is measurable or
590	verifiable here, never for the borrowed authority alone.
591	
592	## How spec-author works
593	
594	1. **Author / grow the relevant requirement** in `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`: find (or open) the requirement the
595	   change belongs to — the intake placement verdict made real: the scenario is the wish's place on
596	   the feature map (SPEC INV-37) — and grow its Context, its User Story, and its named-case criteria, plain
597	   language, anchors at line-ends. Add any new domain noun to the glossary in the same edit. The
598	   code-to-location table is regenerated at freeze by `scripts/build-index.py`; leave it to the builder
599	   rather than editing it by hand. Reuse the existing vocabulary; don't introduce a second word for an existing concept.
600	   Starting fresh? Copy `templates/PRODUCT_SPEC.template.md`. (Template paths resolve from the pack repo —
601	   github.com/happysasha18/live-spec. A standalone install of this skill reads them from a checkout of
602	   that repository, taken with `git clone https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`. They are
603	   deliberately not copied into the skill dir: the pack is the source, a copy would fork the truth.)
604	2. **Ask, don't silently fill.** When the spec needs a decision only the author can make (a threshold, a
605	   policy, desired behavior on an edge), ask the leading question or mark ⟨DECIDE⟩, treating intent as
606	something to confirm; never infer it.
607	3. **Run the completeness pass** (below) on the section just written.
608	4. **Hand off to `product-prover` on the whole spec — the delta included.** The prover catches a
609	   cross-section hole only when *both* sides of the seam are in the document; a surface added in
610	   isolation, or left unlinked, is invisible to it. So re-prove the whole spec whenever a surface is added.
611	5. **Then walk the two layers to the tests** — the architecture doc (nodes owning the spec's facts,
612	   proven with the architecture lens), then the matrix derived node × fact (`spec → prove → architecture
613	   → prove architecture → matrix → test → code`; build-pipeline owns the steps). The spec leads; code
614	   chases it.
615	
616	## The completeness pass — run before declaring a section done
617	
618	Ask each question out loud; a "no" or "don't know" is a gap to fill or mark ⟨DECIDE⟩.
619	
620	- **Entities:** Is every domain noun defined once in the glossary? Does each measure carry a unit + valid
621	  range? Does each entity with a lifecycle list its states?
622	- **Transitions:** For every state, what action leaves it, and who triggers it? Is there a state with no
623	  exit?
624	- **Invariants:** What must never happen here (safety)? What must eventually happen (liveness)? Is each
625	  one stated explicitly?
626	- **Composition:** Does this surface carry state? Under which of the canonical axes (view / mode / tier /
627	  viewport size / persistence-reopen / concurrency / every other live surface) is it shown? For each, is
628	  its state still visible and reversible? Is the transition's effect (preserve / reset / block) stated? If
629	  it persists state, is the older-stored-value × current-code case handled? For every other surface that
630	  can be present at the same time — a sibling on the screen, the surface one step before or after in the
631	  flow — is this surface's behaviour stated while that one is present?
632	- **Facets (feature door):** Did the facet sweep run — does every entry of the canonical facet list end
633	  in a spec sentence, decided or `[default]`-tagged and reported?
634	- **Naming:** Is anything in this section also referred to by another name elsewhere? Unify it.
635	- **Single source of truth:** Does any other document in this repo also claim to be the spec or the matrix
636	  ("source of truth")? If so, demote it to a pointer — two docs claiming authority is undefined when they disagree.
637	- **Honesty:** Is any claim here something the system can't actually deliver, or a guess dressed as a fact?
638	  Mark it ⟨DECIDE⟩ or cut it.
639	- **Readability (human-first, product language):** Does each case name its situation in plain words a
640	  non-author grasps in one read? Are the criteria phrased in product words a person would say, with the
641	  keywords in lowercase italics and no all-capital words outside a code anchor? Are the codes at line-*ends*,
642	  never opening a criterion? Is there any edit-history note in the prose that belongs in the JOURNAL? Does
643	  the spec open with a preamble and a glossary?
644	- **Shape (requirements genre):** Does every requirement carry a Context block, a one-sentence User Story,
645	  and criteria grouped into named cases, numbered continuously through the requirement? Does
646	  `guardrails/check-requirement-shape.py` pass? Is every spine item present inside the requirements or the
647	  glossary? Does the generated code-to-location table match a fresh `scripts/build-index.py` build, with
648	  `guardrails/check-index-generated.py` green? After a restructure: is the anchor set identical to before
649	  (or every delta named)?
650	
651	## The comprehension gate — a changed section passes two layers before it ships
652	
653	A stranger reads a shipped section on first pass, so a changed section clears a comprehension gate: the
654	mechanical lints first, then a panel of fresh cold readers. This gate is spec law and every changed
655	section runs it, closing on two consecutive reads that return zero blocking findings. The text-audit
656	skill carries the loop's method and the reader-prompt — the mechanical lints, the cold reader, and the
657	two-consecutive-clean stopping rule — so run it there rather than restating the loop here. Per changed
658	section the gate is cheap: a small delta puts one glossary entry and a handful of criteria in front of a
659	reader, and the whole document stays out of the reading.
660	
661	**A source hole is a `[GAP: ...]` line, never a filled-in guess.** The source is whatever the criterion is
662	authored from — the person's wish, an older document, or the shipped truth. Where that source states a
663	behaviour and leaves its judge, its measure, or its scope unstated, the criterion names the actor most
664	likely to own the call — the system, or the person the requirement already involves — and carries a `[GAP: ...]` line under
665	it stating what the source left open, so the named actor reads as provisional. Inventing behaviour is
666	forbidden; a gap line is the correct output for a real hole (this is ask-never-guess in the criterion
667	form). Every judgment names its judge and its
668	inputs, and every relational word fills its slots — proportional to what, larger than what, sufficient for
669	what — right where the word stands.
670	
671	## The change record — classify every touched code and hold the size ratchet
672	
673	A spec-touching delivery carries a **delta record**: a JSON file under `docs/deltas/` (one per delivery,
674	e.g. `docs/deltas/2026-07-22-row445.json`) naming every code — every bracket anchor such as `INV-18` —
675	the delivery touched and, for each, exactly one of four kinds. A code names the criterion that carries
676	it, so classifying a code classifies its criterion. The kind names are fixed — they are what the
677	classifier gate `guardrails/check-delta-record.py` reads:
678	
679	- **new** — a code the body of the spec did not carry before;
680	- **sharpen** — a code whose criterion text changed;
681	- **retire** — a code the body no longer carries;
682	- **scenario-only** — a code whose criterion text is unchanged, where only the material around it moved:
683	  its case grouping, its Context prose, or an example. In this one fixed label, "scenario" means those
684	  surroundings of the criterion; it does not carry the person-facing-requirement sense the body of the
685	  spec uses.
686	
687	The classifier diffs the old criteria set against the new one under normalization — whitespace collapsed,
688	italic markers stripped, case folded outside code anchors — and reds where the record and the diff
689	disagree — an added code with no `new` declared, a
690	vanished code with no `retire`, a changed criterion with no `sharpen`. A `sharpen` also proves the old
691	sentence no longer survives anywhere in the new document. The delivery's measured criterion-byte growth
692	(excluding sharpen deltas and glossary additions) stays within the sum of the byte counts of its declared
693	new criteria.
694	
695	Beside the per-delivery record, the whole spec holds a **bytes-per-criterion ratchet**: the byte count of
696	its criterion lines alone, divided by the count of criteria, recorded in `guardrails/spec-ratchet.json` and
697	held by `guardrails/check-size-ratchet.py`. A delivery may lower the bound or leave it; a delivery whose new
698	bytes-per-criterion rises above the recorded bound reds. Raising the bound is a change to the spec's own
699	size requirement, run through the pipeline, never a side effect of a landing.
700	
701	## What spec-author produces
702	
703	A `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` (or an updated section of one) in the requirements genre — a glossary and a body of
704	requirements, each with a Context block, a User Story, and named-case criteria, anchors trailing, closed
705	with a generated code-to-location table — complete against the spine, with surfaces named once and their
706	cross-axis composition stated — ready for `product-prover` to review and for a test matrix to be derived from. The reply also surfaces the ⟨DECIDE⟩ points that could not
707	be resolved and the leading questions behind them.
708	
709	## Anti-patterns (refuse these)
710	
711	- **Speccing a surface on one axis only** — the player described as play/mute/solo with no word on what the
712	  compact view does to it. Always compose.
713	- **Two names for one surface** — "the lanes" and "#stemlanes" as if separate. Unify.
714	- **Filling a gap silently** — inventing a threshold or a behavior the author never decided. Ask or
715	  ⟨DECIDE⟩.
716	- **Speccing after the code** — writing the spec to match what was built. The spec should lead, and the
717	  prover should find the holes before code exists.
718	- **Pinning a drifting version number in prose** — "current version: vX.Y" in a header or README always
719	  goes stale; the version has one home (the VERSION file, the frontmatter) — point there or omit it.
720	  This binds a **derived doc's header** too (ARCHITECTURE.md, TEST_MATRIX.md): a derived doc's header
721	  carries no frozen spec-version number — it names what it derives from, points at the version's one
722	  home (VERSION), and carries a dated "Last reconciled" provenance line, so
723	  a reader never meets a stale number that reads as the current version. A version string has no place
724	  in that header. The lint `tests/test_derived_doc_header_policy.py` holds the two headers to this (row 265).
725	- **A wall of undifferentiated prose** — behaviour run together in paragraphs with no case to land on. The
726	  fix is named cases with numbered criteria, so the reader scans the behaviour; machine-terse fragments are
727	  the opposite failure and get rejected just as hard (see "How it reads").
728	- **Codes opening the line / edit-history in the prose** — `INV-18:` as a criterion's first word, or "in v0.8
729	  we changed…" baked into a rule. Codes trail at line-ends; history goes in the JOURNAL.
730	- **Prose where a criterion belongs** — a behaviour told as a narrative paragraph, leaving the reader no
731	  numbered line to key on. Each rule is a criterion carrying one trigger, one response, and a trailing
732	  anchor, sitting in a named case.
733	- **A hand-edited code-to-location table** — editing the generated Reference table by hand, or letting it
734	  lag the body. The table is generated output (`scripts/build-index.py`); `guardrails/check-index-generated.py`
735	  reds a table that differs from a fresh build. Regenerate it; never hand-edit it.
736	
737	## Pairing with product-prover
738	
739	| | spec-author | product-prover |
740	|---|---|---|
741	| role | writes & grows the spec | reviews the spec |
742	| output | structured `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` sections | findings: gaps, contradictions, missing invariants |
743	| when | starting / adding a feature / a new surface | spec drafted or changed, before tests/code |
744	
745	Author with this skill, review with the prover, then derive matrix + tests. Same primitives on both sides
746	so the handoff is clean.
747

---
name: spec-author
description: Use to start a new product spec, add a feature to an existing spec, or keep a spec in sync with behavior changes. Setting a project up on live-spec comes earlier, at build-pipeline's setup entry. Documenting already-built code after the fact and a prototype sketch that carries no spec stay outside it.
